title: Timing a journey to Paro Tshechu
standfirst: Paro Tshechu moves with the lunar calendar, so the festival sets the dates and the journey follows. How the dates are fixed, when they are announced, and how our two festival journeys fit around them.

body.body: Most holidays start with a date the traveller chooses. A journey to Paro Tshechu starts with a date nobody chooses: it is set by the Bhutanese lunar calendar, and it lands somewhere in March or April depending on the year. Everything else, from the flights to the hotel rooms to the order of the days, is arranged around it.

This is a practical piece about that arrangement: how the dates are worked out, when they become firm, and what it means for when you should write to us. It is written as of 2026, and the parts that change are marked.

A tshechu is held on and around the tenth day of a lunar month, the day associated with Guru Rinpoche. Each district holds its own, in its own month. Paro's belongs to the second month of the Bhutanese calendar: according to the Paro Dzongkhag Administration, the public festival runs over the eleventh to the fifteenth days, with ceremonies inside the dzong beginning on the tenth and closing on the sixteenth.

Because the lunar year does not line up with the Gregorian one, the festival shifts from year to year, sometimes by several weeks. In 2026 it ran from 29 March to 2 April. Some years it falls in the second half of March, some years well into April.

body.title: Paro Tshechu at a glance
rows: Rinpung Dzong and the Deyangkha ground below it
Before dawn on the last day

body.body: The Department of Tourism publishes a list of festival dates for the coming year, marked as tentative. The 2026 list, which gave Paro Tshechu as 29 March to 2 April with the thongdrel on the last day, appeared in April 2025, roughly eleven months ahead. Dates on the list can still move, and they are confirmed closer to the time.

As of September 2026 we have not seen the official list for 2027. Some travel companies already print dates in March 2027 worked out from the lunar calendar, and they may well prove right, but we treat any date as provisional until the Department of Tourism publishes it. When it does, we confirm the departure and write to everyone who has asked.

body.text: How our two festival journeys are built

body.body: We run two journeys around the festival, and both put the festival day near the start rather than at the end. That leaves the rest of the journey to sit with what you have seen, in quieter valleys, instead of flying home the morning after the crowd.

The seven-day Paro Tshechu journey arrives on day one, with a walk through the town and a visit to Kyichu Lhakhang. Day two is the festival, from the morning, at Rinpung Dzong. On day three you return to the dzong without the crowd and climb to Ta Dzong, the National Museum, before driving about an hour and a half to Thimphu. Day four crosses Dochula and continues east to Phobjikha, four to five hours in all, and day five is spent in that open valley, with Gangtey Goenpa and a nature walk. Day six is the long drive back, five to six hours, and day seven is the walk to Taktsang, 3,120 m and four to five hours, before the flight home.

The five-day festival journey is shorter and gentler. Day one is Paro and Kyichu Lhakhang. Day two is the festival. Day three is the drive to Thimphu, about an hour and a half, for Tashichho Dzong and Buddha Dordenma. Day four goes over Dochula at 3,100 m to Punakha Dzong and Chimi Lhakhang, and day five is the three-hour drive back to Paro and the airport.

In both journeys the festival day is fixed to one of the five days of Paro Tshechu once the dates are confirmed. If there is a particular day you want, most often the last one for the thongdrel, tell us when you first write, because it decides which day the departure begins.

On the final morning a thongdrel, a giant appliqué thangka, is carried out and raised on the wall above the Deyangkha ground. At Paro it shows Guru Rinpoche with his eight manifestations and two consorts. The Paro Dzongkhag Administration puts the unveiling at about three in the morning, and it is rolled up and taken back inside before the sun reaches it. The word is usually translated as liberation on sight: to see it is held to bring blessing.

Seeing it means getting up in the dark and walking down in the cold, with thousands of people who have come for the same reason and who will be quietly making their way to the front. It is not a performance. People bow, touch their heads to the cloth where they can reach it, and leave. Stand to the side, keep your voice low and let people pass.

body.text: Booking ahead, and why rooms go early

body.body: Paro Tshechu draws people from all over the country as well as from abroad, and the valley's hotels are small. The rooms nearest the dzong and the seats on the flights into Paro tend to go first in festival week. Our festival journeys run on the same small family-run hotels as every other departure, so availability matters.

items: We suggest writing nine to twelve months ahead if the festival is the reason for the journey.
Hold your international flights until the date is confirmed on the official calendar, or book tickets that can be changed.
Allow a spare day either side if you can. Flights into Paro depend on the weather in the mountains.
The Sustainable Development Fee is US$ 100 per person per night as of 2026, and the government has set that rate until 31 August 2027.

body.body: All of these, the fee, flight schedules and the festival dates themselves, are checked again each season. They are confirmed in the journey notes we send when a departure is booked.

A tshechu is a religious festival first. The dances are performed by monks and laymen as a blessing, the crowd is there to receive it, and the atsaras, the masked clowns, will make fun of anyone, visitors included. Bhutanese wear their finest kira and gho; visitors should dress smartly and modestly, with long sleeves and no hats in the dzong.

items: Photography of the dances is generally allowed in the courtyard. Do not use a flash, and never step into the dance ground.
Sit where your guide suggests. The front rows fill before dawn and are often kept by families.
Bring a hat for outside the dzong, water, and a layer for the cold hours at either end of the day.

title: The cranes of Phobjikha
standfirst: Every autumn several hundred black-necked cranes fly over the Himalaya to winter in one glacial valley in central Bhutan. What is known about them, how the valley has changed to keep them, and how to watch them well.

body.body: The cranes arrive in the last days of October. People in Phobjikha hear them before they see them, a high bugling carried down from the ridges, and then the birds come in over the pass in small groups and settle on the marsh at the valley floor. For the next four months they are part of the valley's daily life.

The black-necked crane, Grus nigricollis, is a bird of high places. It stands about 1.3 m tall, pale grey, with a black head and upper neck, a small white patch behind the eye and a bare red crown. It breeds in summer on the wetlands of the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau, above about 4,500 m, and in autumn moves down to lower valleys to winter. In Dzongkha it is thrung thrung karmo, a name that also belongs to the folk songs written about it.

The Royal Society for Protection of Nature (RSPN) lists it as Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List. Bhutan holds the largest wintering population outside China, spread across a few sites: Phobjikha in the west, the Chhume and Tang valleys in Bumthang, and Bumdeling in the far east.

body.title: At a glance
rows: Late October to mid February, some into March

body.body: Gangtey Goenpa stands on a low spur above the valley floor. Local belief holds that when the cranes arrive they circle the goenpa three times before landing, as a pilgrim walks around a temple, and that they circle it again when they leave in spring. Some people in the valley understand the three circuits as an offering to the Three Jewels. Whether any given flock does it on any given day is a matter of luck and of who was watching; that the belief is held, and held with affection, is not in doubt.

The cranes are woven into the farming year too. Accounts of the valley describe households that wait for the birds to arrive before sowing winter crops, and their arrival is taken as a good sign for the season. The species is fully protected under Bhutanese law.

RSPN was set up in 1987, and the cranes have been at the centre of its work from the start. The first national count, that year, found 370 birds. The count for the winter of 2024 to 2025, reported by Kuensel in February 2025, was 709, the highest on record, and more than 600 of those were in Phobjikha.

The picture is not the same everywhere. Bumdeling, in Trashi Yangtse, once held about 200 cranes and now holds fewer than 60, after floods damaged its roosting and feeding grounds. In Chhume, Tang and Khotokha only a handful were counted. RSPN and the International Crane Foundation are working together on restoring habitat, with most of the effort going to the places that have lost birds. The count for each winter is usually reported in the spring that follows.

For a long time Phobjikha had no mains electricity, and part of the reason was the cranes. Overhead lines across a marsh are a known danger to large birds flying in low light. When grid electrification was planned, from 2007, with support from the Austrian government, RSPN, the Department of Energy and Bhutan Power Corporation worked out a design that kept the lines out of the birds' flight paths: cables were laid largely underground, lines near the forest were run along the tree line, and the main works were done between April and September, while the cranes were away. Grid power came to the valley from 2010. Until then, RSPN had helped households with solar lighting.

It is a small example of something Bhutanese policy talks about in general terms: the idea that progress should be measured by more than output, and that a valley's wildlife is part of its wealth. Here it cost more, took longer and is now invisible, which was the point.

The Black-necked Crane Festival began in 1998, started by RSPN and run by the valley's own environment management committee. It is held each year on 11 November in the courtyard of Gangtey Goenpa. There are folk songs and masked dances by monks and villagers, songs about conservation, and a crane dance by schoolchildren in costume. The festival exists to raise awareness and to give the community a direct income from the cranes; visitors pay an entry fee that goes towards it.

Our journeys that pass through Phobjikha run in spring and autumn, and the festival falls late in the autumn season. A late autumn journey may find the first cranes on the marsh; if you would like to time a visit to the festival, write and we will tell you what can be arranged that year.

The cranes roost at night standing in shallow water on the marsh and fly out at first light to feed across the valley in small family groups. They are used to farmers, but not to people walking towards them. RSPN runs an information centre on the valley side, with an observation deck, and has built a small hide facing the main roosting ponds, about 100 m from the roost.

items: Watch from the hide, the information centre or the marked trails. Do not walk out onto the marsh.
Keep voices down and torches low in the early morning, when the birds are waking.
Do not follow a group that moves away from you. If they lift their heads and stop feeding, you are too close.
Leave drones at home. Flying one in Bhutan needs official permission, and the valley is a conservation area.
Bring binoculars and warm layers. Winter mornings on the valley floor are below freezing.

body.body: Stay long enough and the valley settles back around you: the birds feeding, the farmers going out, the sound of the cranes across the fields. That, rather than any single photograph, is what the conservation work protects.

title: Sitting with a Lam
standfirst: What meditation with a resident Lam in a Bhutanese monastery is actually like: the room, the posture, the prayers and the silence, and how our meditation journey builds practice day by day.

body.body: People often ask what happens in a meditation session in a Bhutanese monastery. The honest answer is: not very much, and that is the point. You take your shoes off, you sit down, a Lam says a few plain things about how to sit and where to put your attention, and then the room goes quiet. What you do with the quiet is up to you.

This piece describes what that is like, what is asked of you, and what is not. It does not describe a programme at any particular monastery, because the monasteries do not run programmes for visitors. You join what is already happening.

Lam is the Bhutanese word for a lama, a teacher in the Buddhist tradition. Not every monk is a Lam. The title is given to someone with long training, often including years in retreat, who is recognised as able to teach. In a monastery the Lam may lead the community's practice, teach the young monks, and give instruction to the lay people who come to them.

On our journeys, the Lams who lead the sittings are resident in the monasteries we stay near. They are not hired to perform for visitors, and nothing is staged. A Lam agrees to sit with a small group because the practice is their work, and your guide, who arranges it, will usually translate.

A session usually takes place in a lhakhang or an assembly hall. The floor is wooden or covered with mats, and there are low cushions or thin mats to sit on. At the front is the altar, with statues, butter lamps and offerings of water and food. The walls are painted, often floor to ceiling, and the light is low. In the morning there is often the smell of incense and butter lamps, and in winter the room is cold enough that you keep your jacket on.

Visitors sit to the side or at the back, never in the seats the monks use. Shoes come off at the door, hats before that. If the monks are chanting when you arrive, you slip in quietly and sit where you are shown. The chanting itself, deep and rhythmic, sometimes with drums, cymbals or horns, can go on for a long time, and it is fine simply to listen.

Sessions vary, but most follow a similar shape. There may be a short prayer or recitation at the start, which you are welcome to listen to rather than join. Then comes instruction, usually brief and practical: how to sit, what to do with your hands and eyes, and where to place your attention. On our journeys the instruction is in mindfulness of breathing, of feeling and of sensation.

Then the silence. It might last ten minutes or forty. Nobody walks around correcting you. The Lam sits too, and the only sounds are the building, the birds outside and, occasionally, a young monk's lesson carrying across the courtyard. At the end there may be a short dedication, and the Lam may take questions.

items: Posture: sit cross-legged on a cushion if you can do so comfortably. If you cannot, ask for a chair or sit with your back against a wall. Nobody minds, and a straight, relaxed back matters more than crossed legs.
Feet: keep them tucked in or to one side, never pointing at the altar or at the Lam.
Eyes: usually half-open, resting on the floor a little ahead of you. Follow what the Lam says.
Prostrations: you may see monks and Bhutanese visitors prostrate three times before the altar. Join them if you wish; nobody expects it of you.
Questions: keep them simple and practical. How to deal with a wandering mind is a better question than one about metaphysics.

body.body: A monastery is a home, a school and a place of worship at once. The young monks you see have lessons, chores and a day that starts before dawn. The older monks may be in the middle of rituals that have gone on for hundreds of years. Your visit is a small interruption in all of that, and the way to be a good guest is to fit in around it.

Keep your voice low anywhere in the monastery, not only in the hall. Ask before photographing anyone, and do not photograph inside the temples at all. Dress as you would for any temple: arms and legs covered. If you want to make an offering, a small note on the altar is the usual way, and your guide can show you.

Nobody will promise you enlightenment, and you should be wary of anyone who does. The Lams who teach visitors tend to speak plainly and to talk about ordinary things: attention, patience, kindness, what happens when you sit still with your own mind for a while. There are no certificates, no grades and no levels. The first few sittings are often uncomfortable, physically and otherwise. That is normal, and nobody is keeping score.

What people take home tends to be smaller and more durable: a way of sitting that they keep up, a habit of noticing the breath on a busy day, a memory of a cold room full of lamps and a teacher who said very little.

body.text: How the meditation journey builds practice

body.body: Our journey of meditation and Buddhist practice is designed around sitting, not sightseeing. Each day opens with a session and closes with one, and the hours between are held in the same spirit. The practice deepens across ten days rather than all at once.

items: The first evening in Paro: an introduction to the practice and a first sitting before dinner.
Thimphu: a long morning session, then Tashichho Dzong when the monks return to it in the afternoon, and time left unscheduled on purpose.
Over the Dochula pass: a stop to sit among the 108 chortens if the sky is clear.
Punakha: one full day held in silence, from waking until the evening session. It is the day most people remember.
The long drive east to Trongsa: practised as mindfulness of sensation rather than endured.
Bumthang: evening prayers at Kharchu Monastery, joining the hall rather than watching it, and a day up at Tharpaling for a long session with the monks.
Paro again: the walk to Taktsang, with the last sitting on the cliff, and a final short session at first light on the morning you leave.

body.body: Other journeys touch the same practice more lightly. The sacred valleys journey includes evening prayers at Kharchu and time to sit at Tharpaling, and on the Paro Tshechu journey there is a chance to sit at Gangtey Goenpa while the chanting is going on, if the timing allows. On every one of them, if a Lam agrees to sit with you, the instruction is the same: sit down, be still, pay attention, and see what happens.

title: The Divine Madman
standfirst: Drukpa Kunley was a fifteenth-century Tibetan yogi who taught through songs, insults and outrageous behaviour. How his stories are told in Bhutan today, and what lies beneath the laughter.

body.body: Ask a Bhutanese friend for a story about Drukpa Kunley and you will probably get two things: a laugh, and a story you would not repeat to your grandmother. Ask them what it means, and the answer will usually be serious. That gap between the telling and the meaning is the whole of him, and it is why, five centuries after his death, he is still one of the most loved figures in the country.

Drukpa Kunley was born in 1455 into the Gya family of Ralung, the seat of the Drukpa Kagyu school in Tsang, in what is now Tibet, and he died in 1529. His family was a distinguished religious one, but his early life was not easy: his father was killed in a dispute over land within the family. He trained as a monk and, as a young man, gave back his vows.

From then on he lived as a wandering yogi, travelling through Tibet and into the southern valleys that are now Bhutan. He married, and his son, Ngawang Tenzin, founded a family line that would matter in Bhutanese history. He was a serious practitioner in the Mahamudra tradition, the teaching that points directly at the nature of the mind. What made him famous was the way he taught it.

body.text: A teacher who offended people on purpose

body.body: He sang. He drank. He mocked lamas who were more interested in their offerings than their students, and monks who kept the letter of their vows and ignored the spirit. He turned up at solemn gatherings and said what nobody else would say, often in verse, often in the coarsest language he could find. The stories give him a hunting dog named Sachi, and a bow and arrows he carried everywhere.

His own writings make clear what he was aiming at. In a passage quoted in Elizabeth Monson's retelling of his life, he compares practitioners with no real understanding to donkeys dressed in leopard skins, eating the crops. The shocking behaviour was the method. It shook people out of their assumptions, including their assumptions about what a holy man should look like, so that the teaching had somewhere to land.

body.text: Three Kunleys, and how the stories are told

body.body: It helps to know that there are really three Drukpa Kunleys. The first is the historical man, of whom relatively little is certain. The second is the writer: a collection of his own verse and prose survives, written mostly in the first person and generally known as his autobiography. Its first volume was translated into English in 2014 as More Than a Madman.

The third, and the one you will meet in Bhutan, is the hero of the folk tales. These were told and retold in villages for centuries, and in the twentieth century many of them were gathered into a biography by the Bhutanese scholar Geshe Gendun Rinchen, who later served as the sixty-ninth Je Khenpo. Keith Dowman and Sonam Paljor translated it in 1980 as The Divine Madman: The Sublime Life and Songs of Drukpa Kunley, and it is still the book most visitors read.

In the tales he walks into a valley, meets a demon or a proud official or a pretty girl, does something outrageous, and leaves the place changed. Many of them explain something you can still see: why a rock has a certain shape, why a temple stands where it does, why an animal looks the way it does. They are told the way good stories always are, with the teller's own additions, and the details differ from valley to valley. Nobody minds. What matters is that the story is told.

The best known tale explains Bhutan's national animal. A crowd of devotees, the story goes, asked Drukpa Kunley to perform a miracle. He agreed, on the condition that they first bring him a whole cow and a whole goat for lunch, and he ate both, leaving only the bones. Then he took the goat's head, set it on the cow's skeleton, and snapped his fingers. The creature got up and walked away up the mountainside to graze: the takin, with a head like a goat and a body like a cow.

It is a story about a miracle, and it is also a joke about greedy holy men and credulous followers, told with a straight face. Both readings are intended. You can see takin in the preserve at Motithang above Thimphu, and you will very likely hear where it came from.

The first time a visitor sees a large painted phallus beside a farmhouse door, often with ribbons, sometimes with a face, the reaction is usually surprise. In rural Bhutan it is ordinary. The painted and carved phallus is a protective sign, meant to turn away the evil eye and malicious gossip. Carved wooden ones hang from the eaves at the four corners of a house, sometimes crossed with a sword, and some are set out in fields.

The symbol is associated with Drukpa Kunley, whose tales call it his thunderbolt of wisdom and use it to subdue demons. Scholars have suggested the protective phallus may be older than Buddhism in the region and that his legend gave it a Buddhist meaning. It is less common in towns now, and some urban Bhutanese find it old-fashioned. In the villages it is not a joke, and it is best not treated as one. Ask before photographing a house, as you would anywhere.

Punakha is where the stories settle. Tradition holds that Drukpa Kunley subdued a demoness who had been troubling travellers on the Dochula pass, pursued her down the valley and pinned her beneath a rock on the low hill where a chorten was built. In 1499 a temple, Chimi Lhakhang, was founded beside it by Ngawang Chogyal, the fourteenth Drukpa hierarch. Couples from across Bhutan and beyond still come there to ask for children, and are blessed with a wooden phallus kept in the temple.

His family line also runs through Bhutanese history. His son's descendants included Tsewang Tenzin, who gave the Zhabdrung the site of Tango monastery, and Tsewang Tenzin's son, Tenzin Rabgye, who became the fourth Druk Desi, the head of the civil government, in the seventeenth century. The madman's great-grandson helped govern the country that grew up around the dzongs.

Visitors sometimes come away thinking of Drukpa Kunley as a bawdy local curiosity. Bhutanese generally do not. To them he is a realised master who happened to be very funny, and whose outrageousness was a kindness: a way of reaching people that solemnity could not. When your guide tells you one of his stories, listen for the second meaning. There nearly always is one.

title: A hot stone bath
standfirst: The dotsho, Bhutan's hot stone bath: river stones heated in a wood fire, a wooden tub with artemisia in the water, and an evening soak after a long day on the road or the trail.

body.body: The first thing you notice is the smoke. Somewhere behind the farmhouse a wood fire has been burning for a long time, with a heap of river stones set into the heart of it. By the time you arrive the stones are too hot to go near, and the wooden tub in the bath house beside it is full of cold water, waiting for them.

This is the dotsho, the Bhutanese hot stone bath, and it is one of the few things on a journey here that asks nothing of you except to sit still in warm water. It is also older than most of the buildings you will visit.

A dotsho is a bath heated not by a boiler but by stones. Large river stones, roughly the size of a pomelo, are heated in an open fire outside the bath house. When they are ready they are lifted out and dropped through a hatch in the wall into a closed-off section at one end of the tub. A wooden partition separates them from the bather, so the heat reaches you through the water and there is no danger of touching a stone.

The water hisses and steams as each stone goes in, and the heat spreads outward from the partition. As the water cools, more stones are added. You say when you would like it hotter, and someone outside feeds in another stone. On the water floats a handful of leaves, most often artemisia, a wormwood with a sharp, clean smell that fills the small room.

The Department of Tourism traces the custom to at least the seventh century, influenced later by Tibetan medicine and by Indian Ayurvedic practice. Bhutanese have used it for joint pains, tired muscles and a range of other complaints, and above all as a way to get warm and stay warm through a mountain winter. How much of the healing is the minerals, the herbs or simply the heat is a question for doctors rather than for us, and we make no claims for it beyond that it is very pleasant.

body.title: The dotsho at a glance
rows: A wooden tub heated by fire-heated river stones
A farmhouse, a village bath house or a hotel
An evening after a long drive or walk

body.body: The traditional place for a dotsho is outside a farmhouse, in the back garden or down by the river where the stones come from. That is still where the best of them are: a small timber bath house, a tub made from planks, the fire outside tended by someone from the family. It is an act of hospitality as much as a service. The fire has to be lit and the stones heated long before you arrive, and the host's time is a large part of what you are being offered.

Hot stone baths are now also found in many hotels, from small family-run places to large resorts, and in some villages there are bath houses built for visitors. They work in the same way. The farmhouse version is simpler, often darker and smokier, and closer to what Bhutanese families have always done.

It is a winter custom first. Bhutanese take a dotsho most often in the cold months, and the Department of Tourism describes it as especially good in the cold season. For visitors it works in any month, and it is most welcome in spring and autumn in the higher valleys, where the evenings turn cold quickly.

body.text: How it fits into a day

body.body: A hot stone bath belongs at the end of a day, not the start of one. It is heavy on the body in a good way, and afterwards most people want food and sleep rather than anything else. On our Paro Tshechu journey it is offered on the first evening, if you want one, to let the flight and the altitude settle. On other journeys it fits well after the long drive between valleys, after the walk to Taktsang, or on the last evening before you fly home.

Tell your guide early if you would like one. The stones need a long time in the fire, so a bath is arranged ahead rather than decided on the spot. Allow around an hour from arriving to leaving, with half of that in the water.

items: Ask whether the bath is private or shared, and bring swimwear if you are unsure. Farmhouse baths are often taken one person or one couple at a time.
Shower or wash before you get in, if the farmhouse has somewhere to do so. Keep soap out of the tub; it is for soaking.
Keep your hands and feet away from the partition. The stones on the other side are very hot and the wood close to them can be too.
If you want the water hotter or cooler, say so. Asking for another stone is quite normal.
You may be offered ara, the local spirit, or butter tea. Butter tea is a good choice. See below on ara.
Thank the family. The work that went into the fire is the real gift.

body.body: A hot stone bath is a very hot bath, and the ordinary cautions for saunas and hot tubs apply. We are not doctors, and if any of the points below applies to you, ask your own before you take one.

items: Pregnancy: the NHS notes that you may choose to avoid saunas and hot tubs in pregnancy because of the risks of overheating, dehydration and fainting, particularly in the first twelve weeks.
Heart conditions, and high or low blood pressure: very hot water affects circulation and blood pressure. Talk to your doctor first, and keep the water warm rather than hot.
Standing up: getting out of hot water can make anyone light-headed. Stand slowly, and have something to hold on to.
Alcohol: a glass of ara in a hot bath is traditional, but alcohol and heat together make fainting more likely, and at altitude it is best avoided on your first days in any case.
Your first night at altitude: if you have a headache or feel unwell from the altitude, keep the bath short and not too hot, or leave it for another evening.
Drink plenty of water before and after, and do not take a bath straight after a heavy meal.

body.body: If you feel dizzy, sick or faint, get out, sit down and tell your guide. Your guide carries a first-aid kit and will know the house.

Most travellers remember the details: the smell of wood smoke and artemisia, the hiss of the stones, the light from a small window, the warmth coming in waves from one end of the tub. It is not a spa treatment and does not try to be. It is a very old way of getting warm at the end of a cold day, offered by people who have been doing it for generations, and it is at its best taken slowly, with nothing else planned for the evening.

title: What to pack for Bhutan
standfirst: Clothes for dzongs and a thousand metres of temperature change, boots for Taktsang, plugs, cash and cards, a local SIM, and what to leave at home, with a checklist.

body.body: Packing for Bhutan comes down to two facts. The valleys you move between differ by a thousand metres and more, so a warm afternoon in Punakha can be followed by a frosty night in Bumthang. And most days include a dzong or temple, where arms and legs must be covered. Pack for both and you are most of the way there.

Some of the heavier kit is already taken care of. On all our journeys we lend each traveller a down jacket, an all-season sleeping bag and a duffel bag, so none of those needs to come in your luggage.

On temple days you need long trousers, or a skirt or dress below the knee, and a top with sleeves. A collared shirt is the safe choice for men. Shorts, vests and flip-flops are not allowed through the gate. Choose a few pieces that look tidy and wash easily, and you can wear the same outfit into a dzong in the morning and on a valley walk in the afternoon.

Shoes come off at the door of every temple room, so slip-ons or boots with quick laces save time over a day. Many travellers buy a kira or gho in Thimphu or Paro and wear it for a festival. It is not expected, but it is welcomed.
Whatever the month, dress in layers you can add and remove through the day: a base layer, a warm fleece or light insulated jacket, and a waterproof shell.

items: Spring and autumn (March to May, September to November): mild days around the low twenties in Thimphu, cold nights, and colder still in Bumthang and Phobjikha. A fleece, a waterproof, a warm hat for evenings, and sun protection for the clear days.
Summer (June to August): warm and wet. A good rain jacket, quick-drying trousers, and a small umbrella for walking between temples. Long sleeves help with insects on lower trails.

Winter (December to February): cold, dry and bright. Thermal base layers, warm gloves and a hat, and a warm layer for sleeping, since rooms in the central valleys rely on heaters. The loaned down jacket earns its place.
The Jomolhari trek (autumn): proper cold-weather layers for nights well below freezing at 4,000 m and above. We send a full trek kit list with the journey notes.

body.text: Footwear for Taktsang and the trails

body.body: The walk to Taktsang is the one that tests footwear. The path climbs through pine forest on dirt and loose stone, then drops to a waterfall and climbs again by stone steps, and the round trip is four to five hours. It is dusty in dry weather and slick after rain. Light walking boots or trail shoes with a good grip are right; new boots are not.

Bring walking poles if you use them, especially for the descent, and a small day pack with water, a warm layer and a rain shell. For the Jomolhari trek you need broken-in waterproof trekking boots with ankle support, and a pair of camp shoes for the evenings.

Mains supply is 230 volts at 50 Hz. Sockets are mostly round-pin: the three-pin type D, which also takes the two-pin type C found on European plugs. Some newer hotels fit universal sockets. A universal adapter covers every case, and a small extension lead or multi-port charger helps when a room has only one socket. On the trek there is no mains power, so bring a power bank.

The currency is the ngultrum, pegged to the Indian rupee, and rupees are accepted almost everywhere. Most hotels, restaurants and handicraft shops in the towns take cards. As of 2026, ATMs in Thimphu, Paro and Punakha accept Visa and Mastercard, but they thin out quickly as you travel east, and foreign cards usually pay a fee per withdrawal. Carry enough cash for the central valleys, in small notes, for offerings, snacks, tips and village shops.

Mobile coverage is good across most of the country, and international roaming works with most operators. For local data, both B-Mobile and TashiCell sell tourist SIM cards from counters at Paro airport, and you need your passport to register one. Hotels and cafés have wi-fi. On the Jomolhari route there are stretches with no signal for a day or more, and we tell you in advance where they are.

body.body: If you are visiting a farmhouse or staying with a family, a small gift from home is a kind gesture: something from your region, a book of photographs, good tea. title: Fifteen days to Jomolhari
standfirst: The Jomolhari trek stage by stage: ten days on the trail from the ruins at Drukgyel to the road above Thimphu, over two passes above 4,800 m, with rest days at the foot of the mountain and at Lingshi.

body.body: Jomolhari stands on the border between Bhutan and Tibet at 7,326 m. Nobody climbs it now: Bhutan does not permit mountaineering on its high peaks, out of respect for the deities held to live on them, and Jomolhari is regarded as the dwelling of the goddess Jomo. The trek that bears its name does not go up the mountain. It walks to the foot of it, crosses the high ground beside it, and comes down the other side into the valley above Thimphu.

Our version takes fifteen days. Ten of them are on the trail, and two of those ten are rest days in camp. It is not the shortest way to do the route. It is built that way so the body has time to catch up with the altitude.

body.title: At a glance
rows: 15 days, 14 nights; 10 on the trail, 2 of them rest days
Drukgyel, Paro valley, to Dodina, above Thimphu

body.text: Before the trek: two days in Paro

body.body: The journey begins in Paro at 2,200 m, with Kyichu Lhakhang and a slow afternoon. Day two is the walk to Taktsang, 3,120 m and about five hours there and back. On a cultural journey that walk comes at the end. Here it comes first, taken early, as acclimatisation as much as pilgrimage: a climb of several hundred metres and a return to sleep low, which is how the body is best introduced to height. The rest of the day is for checking kit and resting.

body.text: Up the Pa Chhu to Jangothang, and a day at rest

body.body: Day three starts at the ruined dzong at Drukgyel, at the head of the Paro valley. The first day's walk is gentle, about six hours through farmland and pine along the Pa Chhu, to camp at Shana, 2,870 m.

Day four is the first long one: about eight hours up the river valley to Soi Thangthangkha at 3,610 m. The forest closes in and then opens, and if the cloud lifts, Jomolhari shows itself for the first time. Day five is shorter, about five hours, and climbs above the tree line into yak pasture, past a small army post, to Jangothang at 4,080 m. The camp sits beneath the face of the mountain.

Day six is spent at Jangothang. It is called a rest day, and it is one, but it also does a job. Sleeping two nights at the same height before going higher is one of the plainest rules of acclimatisation. You can walk up to the Tshophu lakes above camp, which takes you higher for a few hours and brings you back down to sleep, or you can sit outside the tent and look at the mountain. Either counts.

This is also the part of the trek where wildlife is most likely. Takin and blue sheep graze the upper slopes of this region, and the route lies within Jigme Dorji National Park. Seeing them is never certain; the herders' camps, and tea in them if the season is right, are more likely.

body.text: Over the Nyile La to Lingshi

body.body: Day seven is the high point of the trek and one of its hardest days: about eight hours, up to the Nyile La at 4,930 m, with Jomolhari, Jichu Drake and Tsherimgang behind you as you climb. The pass is often windy and the final stretch is slow. From the top it is a long descent to Lingshi.

Day eight is the second rest day. Lingshi Dzong, on its ridge above the valley, was built in the seventeenth century after a victory over Tibetan forces, commanding the route to the border, and it has been damaged by earthquake and restored since. It still houses monks and a small administrative office. The village below is lived in all year, which at this height means long winters and a short growing season. The day is for the dzong, for the village and for the people who live up here.

body.text: The Yale La, and down to Thimphu

body.body: Day nine is the longest day of the trek: about nine hours over the Yale La at 4,820 m, the last high pass, with the ranges along the Tibetan border to the north, and then a long descent into the Thimphu Chhu valley to camp at Shodu. It is the day the trek turns for home, and most of what remains is downhill.

From there the trek loses height steadily. Day ten follows the river down through rhododendron and birch, past waterfalls, to the ruins of Barshong Dzong at 3,710 m, about six hours. Day eleven is shorter, about five hours, to Dolam Kencho at 3,290 m, and the air grows noticeably thicker as you go. Day twelve is the last walking day, about four hours out to the road head at Dodina, and a short drive into Thimphu at 2,320 m. A hot shower, and a bed.

Day thirteen is a gentle day in Thimphu: Tashichho Dzong and Buddha Dordenma, taken slowly while the legs recover. Day fourteen is the drive of about an hour and a half back to Paro, with the afternoon free, and day fifteen is the transfer to the airport.

body.text: The crew, the camp and the animals

body.body: You carry a day pack and nothing else. Tents, sleeping mats, the kitchen and a dining shelter travel with the trek, carried by ponies and led by their handlers. On some high sections of the route, depending on the season and the herders, yaks may take the loads instead. The crew goes ahead with the ponies and sets camp, so it is usually up by the time you walk in.

items: Your guide is licensed and walks with the group every day.
A proper first-aid kit travels with the trek. If anyone needs to go down, the group goes down.
A down jacket, an all-season sleeping bag and a duffel bag are lent to you for the trek.
There are stretches with no mobile signal for a day or more. We tell you in advance where.
Tipping is never expected. Travellers who give something at the end usually include the cook, the assistant cook and the horsemen.

body.text: When to go, and how fit to be

body.body: The trek runs in autumn. The monsoon has cleared by then, the peaks are at their sharpest and the days are usually dry, while the nights at the high camps are cold, often at or below freezing. Snow can fall on the passes at either end of the season, and the guide decides each morning whether a crossing is safe.

You do not need mountaineering experience. You do need to be able to walk for six to nine hours, several days running, on rough ground and at altitude, and still enjoy it. The best preparation is walking itself: long days in hills, back to back, carrying a light pack. Talk to your doctor before booking, and tell us about any condition that altitude might affect. The Sustainable Development Fee is US$ 100 per person per night as of 2026; fees, permits and trail conditions are checked each season and confirmed in the journey notes we send when a departure is booked.

title: Altitude in Bhutan: what to expect and how we plan for it
standfirst: How high Bhutan's valleys and passes are, what altitude sickness is, how our journeys and the Jomolhari trek are paced to acclimatise, and when the answer is to go down.

body.body: Almost every journey in Bhutan begins with a jump in height. You fly from a hub close to sea level and step off the plane in Paro at about 2,200 m. For most people the only effect that first afternoon is a little breathlessness on the stairs. Altitude is still the single thing that shapes how we plan our journeys more than any other, and it is worth understanding before you come.

This is general information, not medical advice. If you have a heart or lung condition, are pregnant, have had altitude sickness before, or are walking the Jomolhari trek, talk to your doctor or a travel clinic before you book.

The pattern matters more than any single number. On our valley, festival and meditation journeys you sleep between about 1,200 m and 2,900 m, and the higher points (Dochula, the Pele La, Taktsang and Tharpaling) are reached by day and left the same day. The Jomolhari trek is different: you sleep above 4,000 m for several nights and cross passes close to 5,000 m.

As you go higher the air holds less oxygen with each breath. At around 3,000 m the oxygen you breathe in is only about two thirds of what it is at sea level, and the body needs days to adjust. The NHS notes that altitude sickness usually becomes a risk above about 2,500 m, and it does not depend on fitness: a marathon runner can be affected and a sedentary walker spared.

The common, mild form is acute mountain sickness. Symptoms usually start within hours of arriving at a new height, often during or after the first night, and feel like a hangover: headache, loss of appetite, nausea, tiredness, dizziness and poor sleep. If you stop climbing and rest at the same height, it usually settles within a day or two.

There are two rarer, serious forms. High altitude pulmonary oedema is fluid on the lungs: breathlessness even at rest, a cough, and sometimes frothy or bloodstained spit. High altitude cerebral oedema is swelling of the brain: confusion, drowsiness, and clumsiness or loss of balance, like someone who is very drunk. Both are emergencies, and the treatment for both is to descend at once.

The principle behind acclimatisation is to go up gradually. Current guidance from the Wilderness Medical Society and the CDC is that above 3,000 m you should raise the height at which you sleep by no more than about 500 m a day, and take a rest day, sleeping at the same height, every three or four days. The NHS also advises against going from below 1,200 m to above 3,500 m in a single day.

On the valley journeys that means the first days are deliberately gentle. Arrival days in Paro are for a short walk, a temple and rest, not a climb. Taktsang comes late in most itineraries, when you have had a week at 2,000 m to 2,900 m, and even then the advice is to take the path slowly: it is the altitude, not the distance, that tires people. Tharpaling at 3,600 m is a day visit from the Bumthang valley.

On the Jomolhari trek we build in more. There are two nights in the Paro valley first, with the walk to Taktsang on the second day as acclimatisation. The trek starts at Drukgyel and sleeps at Shana, at 2,870 m, and Soi Thangthangkha, at 3,610 m, which is the biggest single gain on the route. The guidance itself recognises that terrain sometimes forces a larger step, and on this route there is nowhere to camp in between. The next night is at Jangothang, 4,080 m, followed by a full rest day there before the Nyile La at 4,930 m, and a second rest day at Lingshi after the pass.

body.text: Symptoms, and when to go down

body.body: The rules are short, and your guide and trek crew hold to them.

items: Tell your guide about any symptom, however small. A headache that goes unmentioned is the most common way a mild problem becomes a serious one.
Never go higher to sleep while you have symptoms of altitude sickness, however minor they seem.
If symptoms do not improve with rest at the same height, or get worse, go down. The NHS suggests a descent of 300 to 1,000 m; often a few hundred metres makes a clear difference.
Breathlessness at rest, confusion, drowsiness or unsteadiness means going down immediately, day or night, with someone alongside you.
Painkillers such as paracetamol or ibuprofen may ease a headache, but they do not treat the cause. Feeling better on a tablet is not a reason to climb.

body.body: We carry a first-aid kit on every journey, and on a trek it is a full one. If anyone needs to go down, we go down, and the rest of the group's plans come second. On the high route there are stretches with no phone signal, and your insurance should cover evacuation by helicopter; see our guide to planning a first journey.

body.text: Medication: a conversation with your doctor

body.body: There is a prescription medicine, acetazolamide, that speeds acclimatisation and can reduce the chance and severity of acute mountain sickness. It does not suit everyone and has side effects, and whether you should take it, and how, is a decision for your doctor or a travel clinic, not for us or for a forum online. The NHS suggests speaking to a GP or travel clinic if you have had altitude sickness before or are going high quickly.

The same conversation is the place to raise anything else relevant: heart or lung disease, sleep apnoea, pregnancy, or any regular medicines. The CDC advises that travellers with conditions like these see a doctor with experience of altitude before they go. Bring your own prescriptions in their original packaging, and enough for the whole journey plus a few days.

Fitness does not protect you from altitude sickness, but it makes the days far more enjoyable. The walk to Taktsang is about five hours up and down with a steep final stretch of stone steps. Trek days on the Jomolhari route run from four hours to nine, and the day over the Nyile La is eight.

items: Walk hills or stairs regularly for two or three months before you come, carrying a light day pack.
If you are trekking, build up to several long days in a row, and wear the boots you will trek in.
On arrival, go slowly for the first two days even if you feel well. Walk at a pace where you can still talk.
Drink enough water to stay well hydrated, and avoid alcohol for the first 48 hours at a new height, as both the NHS and CDC advise.
Do not take sleeping tablets at altitude unless a doctor who knows where you are going has prescribed them.

body.body: Guidance on altitude illness is revised from time to time, and the notes we send for your journey reflect the current advice as of your departure. None of this is meant to alarm. Most travellers on our valley journeys notice nothing worse than a quick breath on the stairs, and those who walk the high route slowly are the ones who reach the pass feeling well.

title: Dress and etiquette in dzongs and temples
standfirst: What to wear in a dzong or temple, why hats and shoes come off, walking clockwise, making an offering, behaving at a tshechu, and the rules on tobacco, photography and drones.

body.body: Most of the buildings you visit in Bhutan are in daily use. A dzong holds the district's offices and its monk body under one roof. A lhakhang is someone's place of worship before it is anything else. Nobody expects a visitor to know every custom, and your guide will steer you, but a few habits make the difference between being tolerated and being welcome.

The rule in any dzong, temple or monastery is simple: arms and legs covered. That means long trousers, or a skirt or dress that falls below the knee, and a top with sleeves. Collared shirts are the norm for men, and a shirt without a collar should have long sleeves. Shorts, vests, short skirts and flip-flops are not allowed through the gate, and the attendants do turn people away.

Some dzongs have tightened their rules. At Trongsa, new monument guidelines came into force on 1 January 2026 requiring formal dress with shoulders and knees covered. The simplest approach is to dress on every temple day as if for a smart office: a collared shirt or a blouse, long trousers or a long skirt, and shoes you can take off easily.

Bhutanese wear national dress in a dzong, the gho for men and the kira for women, with a ceremonial scarf over the shoulder, the kabney for men and the rachu for women. Visitors are not expected to wear either the dress or the scarf. If you buy a kira or gho and want to wear it, most Bhutanese take it as a compliment, and your guide will show you how it is tied.

body.title: Temple dress, as of 2026
rows: Covered; collared shirt or long sleeves
Long trousers, or a skirt below the knee
Hats and caps off before you enter
Shoes off at the door of a temple room

body.body: Take off your hat before you go through the gate, and your sunglasses with it. At the threshold of a temple room, take off your shoes and leave them outside with everyone else's. Keep socks on if the floor is cold; nobody minds. Large bags are left outside or with the guide, and at Taktsang they are left at the entrance.

Photography is the rule people most often get wrong. In most dzongs you may photograph the courtyards and the outside of the buildings, but not the inside of any temple, shrine room or assembly hall. A few places allow more and a few allow less, and the rule differs from building to building. Ask your guide before you lift a camera or a phone, every time. Never photograph monks at prayer without asking, and never use flash near murals.

Walk clockwise around anything sacred: a chorten, a temple, a mani wall carved with prayers, the inner sanctum of a lhakhang. In practice that means keeping the sacred object on your right. At the Memorial Chorten in Thimphu you will see this all day, with people walking round it from first light until dusk.

Prayer wheels are turned clockwise too, with the right hand, as you walk past them. Each holds a roll of printed prayers, and turning it is understood as reciting them. You are welcome to turn them. The large wheels inside some temples are heavier than they look; push slowly and let them come round.

Inside a temple room, keep your voice low and move slowly. Do not sit with your feet pointing at the altar, at a Lam or at another person, which is considered disrespectful; sit cross-legged, or tuck your feet to one side. Point at something with an open hand rather than a single finger. Do not climb on or lean against chortens, statues or old walls.

There is no charge for entering most temples beyond any entrance fee at the gate, and no expectation that you give. If you want to make an offering, a small note placed on the altar or in the offering box is the usual form, and a butter lamp can be lit for a small donation to the caretaker. A monk may pour a little holy water into your palm. The custom is to sip it and pass the rest over your head; if you would rather not drink, touch it to your head only.

Monks are generally relaxed and often curious about visitors. Speak to them as you would to anyone, ask before photographing, and keep physical contact to a minimum. Women visiting are welcome throughout nearly every temple, but occasionally a goenkhang, a chapel of the protector deities, is closed to women, or to all visitors. Your guide will tell you at the door. The reason is religious, not personal.

A tshechu is a religious festival before it is a spectacle. The cham dances are teachings and blessings, and the crowd is there to receive them. Dress as you would for a temple, or better: the whole valley wears its finest kira and gho for the festival, not for visitors, and scruffy clothes stand out.

items: Never walk across the courtyard while the dances are going on. Go round the edge.
Keep your seat to the side or behind, and leave space at the front for the elderly and for families who have come for the blessing.
Photograph the dances from where you sit. Do not step into the dance ground for a closer shot, and never use flash.
The atsara, the masked clowns, will tease the crowd and may pick on a visitor. Laugh along; it is part of their role.
When the thongdrel is unrolled at dawn, people queue to touch their heads to its hem. Join the queue quietly or stand back and watch.

body.body: Tobacco has an unusual history in Bhutan. Its sale was banned outright until the Tobacco Control Act was amended in 2021, and sale is now legal. Smoking is still prohibited in public places, including markets, restaurants, bars, public gatherings and festivals, the airport and public transport, and a hotel may choose to be entirely smoke-free. Never smoke anywhere near a dzong, temple or chorten.

Visitors may bring in a limited quantity of tobacco for personal use, with duty payable at customs. As of 2026 the allowance commonly given is 200 cigarettes, and anything you bring must be declared on arrival. Keep the customs receipt with you in case you are asked for it.

Drones are simpler: as of 2026 the Department of Tourism says tourists are generally not permitted to bring them into Bhutan. Flying is approved only for official purposes. If you arrive with one, declare it at customs, where it will normally be held until you leave. Leave it at home.
These rules are checked each season, and anything that has changed for your dates is set out in the journey notes. The rest is courtesy, and it is noticed.

title: The four harmonious friends
standfirst: An elephant, a monkey, a hare and a bird, standing one on another beneath a tree. Where the picture comes from, what it teaches, and why you will see it on walls all over Bhutan.

body.body: Once you have noticed it, you see it everywhere. On the wall beside a dzong doorway, in the porch of a village lhakhang, above the altar in a farmhouse, painted on a hotel corridor, printed on a tea cup in a Thimphu shop: an elephant, a monkey on its back, a hare on the monkey, and a bird on top, all beneath a tree heavy with fruit. In Dzongkha it is Thuenpa Puenzhi, usually translated as the four harmonious friends or the four friends in harmony.

It is probably the best known story in Bhutan, and it is told to children long before they could explain what it means. It is worth knowing before you travel, because it explains a good deal about how people here think about age, respect and getting along.

There are several versions, and Bhutanese tellers do not always agree on the details. In the one most often told, four animals live near a great tree in a forest near Varanasi. They begin to argue over whose tree it is, or, in gentler tellings, over which of them should be honoured as the eldest. They settle it by asking each other what the tree looked like when they first saw it.

The elephant says that when he was young the tree was a bush, so small he walked over it and its top brushed his belly. The monkey says that when he first came, he could eat from its highest branches sitting on the ground. The hare says he remembers it as a sapling, and nibbled its first leaves. Then the bird speaks: he once ate a fruit from another tree, he says, and dropped the seed here, and this tree grew from it.

The bird is the eldest, and the others accept it. From then on the elephant carries the monkey, the monkey carries the hare and the hare carries the bird, so that the eldest sits highest and can reach the fruit, which is then shared among all four. In some versions the bird goes on to teach the others to keep the five basic precepts, and the other animals of the forest follow their example.

The story is much older than Bhutan. Its source is the Tittira Jataka, one of the Jataka tales of the Buddha's former lives, in which the animals are three rather than four: a partridge, a monkey and an elephant, living beside a banyan tree. The partridge proves himself the eldest in the same way, by having planted the tree from a seed.

The Jataka also records why the Buddha told it. A group of monks had gone ahead and taken all the lodgings in a town, and his senior disciple Sariputta, finding nowhere to stay, spent the night beneath a tree. The Buddha asked the monks who ought to have the best lodging, water and food, and when they could not agree he told them the story of the three animals. The rule he gave afterwards was that these things go by seniority in the order. In the tale's closing identification, the partridge was the Buddha in a former life, the monkey Sariputta, and the elephant Moggallana.
As the story travelled into Tibet, Bhutan and Mongolia, a hare joined the group. The version painted in Bhutan today is the four-animal one.

body.text: What it is taken to mean

body.body: The plainest reading is the one in the Jataka: respect goes by age, not by size or strength. The elephant is the largest and the youngest, and he is the one at the bottom, carrying the others. That turns an ordinary expectation upside down, and it is the reason the picture is so easy to remember.

The second reading is cooperation. None of the four can reach the fruit alone, and none of them is doing the work on their own: each supports one and is supported by another. In 2005 Kuensel asked several Bhutanese scholars and teachers what the painting meant to them. Dasho Lam Sanga described it as a picture of interdependence despite the differences in size and strength between the animals, and compared the four animals to the four pillars of Gross National Happiness. Thinley Wangchuk, a former Dzongkha teacher, told the paper that wherever the picture of the four brothers is displayed, the ten virtues are held to increase.

Others read the four animals as parts of a person, or as a family: elders and young, each with a place. None of these readings excludes the others, and in conversation Bhutanese will move between them without feeling any contradiction.

body.text: Where you will see it on a journey

body.body: The Kuensel piece listed the places the painting turns up: altars and sitting rooms in homes, lhakhangs, monasteries and dzongs. A journey takes you into most of them. Look for it in the painted porches and galleries of dzongs and temples, where it keeps company with the guardian kings and the wheel of life, and in the altar rooms of the farmhouses you visit.

items: In dzong courtyards and galleries, among the other protective and teaching murals.
In the entrance porches of village temples.
In farmhouses you visit, often in the altar room.
In the handicraft shops of Thimphu and Paro, on thangkas, carved panels, cups and cards.

body.body: Painting is one of the thirteen traditional arts, the Zorig Chusum, and this is one of its most familiar subjects. Look at a few versions and you will notice the differences: the bird drawn differently from one painter to the next, the monkey sometimes painted red, the tree in fruit or in flower. The arrangement, eldest at the top, never changes.

Guides on our journeys often reach for the four friends when a traveller asks something large: why the eldest at a table is served first, or how a country can say it measures happiness. The story does in a minute what a lecture could not. It is familiar, it is funny, and it carries its meaning in a picture you can point at on the nearest wall.

It is also a good picture to carry home. Bhutan is not a country without disagreement, and nobody here would claim that it is. But the idea that a household, a village or a nation works best when each part carries another, and when age is honoured ahead of strength, is not only painted on walls. Watch who is served first at a family meal, or who is offered the seat, and you will see the picture again.

title: When to visit Bhutan
standfirst: Bhutan season by season: spring rhododendrons and Paro Tshechu, the green monsoon, clear autumn skies for trekking, and cold bright winters with the cranes in Phobjikha.

body.body: There is no bad month to be in Bhutan, but there are months that suit particular journeys. The short answer most people give is spring or autumn, and it is a fair one. The longer answer depends on what you want to see, how high you are going and how much rain you mind.

Height matters as much as the calendar. Punakha lies at about 1,200 m and stays mild even in January. Bumthang, at 2,600 m, has frost on most winter nights. The camp at Jangothang on the Jomolhari trek is at 4,080 m, where even an autumn night is well below freezing. A single journey can cross all of these in a week, so it helps to think of weather by altitude as much as by month.

rows: June to August, with July the peak

body.body: As a rough guide, Punakha runs several degrees warmer than Thimphu at any time of year, and Bumthang and Phobjikha several degrees colder. Passes such as Dochula, at 3,100 m, are colder again and often windy.

Spring is when the valleys turn green and the hillsides flower. Bhutan has dozens of species of rhododendron, and from March into May they come out in stages, lower slopes first, the high passes last. Magnolia flowers in the forests around the same time, and in Punakha the jacaranda turns lilac around the dzong. The botanical park near Dochula holds a rhododendron festival each April; in 2026 it falls on 13 and 14 April.

It is also festival season. Paro Tshechu, the best known of the valley festivals, falls in spring each year on dates set by the lunar calendar; in 2026 it runs from 29 March to 2 April in the courtyard of Rinpung Dzong, ending with the thongdrel unrolled before dawn. Days are mild and good for walking. The one drawback is haze: by late April the distant peaks are often hidden by afternoon, and the clearest mountain views belong to autumn and winter.

The monsoon reaches Bhutan in early summer and brings most of the year's rain between June and September. It is not constant. Many days have dry spells, and the rain often arrives in the afternoon or overnight. But the high peaks spend most of the season in cloud, trails at lower altitude have leeches, and landslides sometimes close a road for hours while crews clear it.

In exchange the country is at its greenest, the rice is being planted in terraces up the valley sides, and there are far fewer visitors. It suits journeys where the landscape is not the point. Our meditation journey runs year round, and in summer the long sittings in the monasteries and the day of silence in Punakha are, if anything, easier to keep. If you travel in these months, allow a little slack in the itinerary and bring a good rain shell.

When the monsoon clears, usually in late September, the air sharpens and the peaks come back into view. October and November are the clearest, driest and most settled months of the year, which is why they are also the busiest. The rice is harvested and laid to dry, and the weather suits long walks and high passes.

The big autumn festival is Thimphu Tshechu, in the courtyard of Tashichho Dzong; in 2026 it runs from 21 to 23 September. Bumthang's Jambay Lhakhang Drup follows in late October or November, falling from 26 to 29 October in 2026. Autumn is also the main season for high treks. Our Jomolhari trek runs only in autumn, when the monsoon has gone, the nights are cold and dry, and the Nyile La at 4,930 m is at its most reliable.

Winter in the central valleys is cold at night and bright by day. From October to February the air is at its clearest, and on a good morning at Dochula the whole eastern Himalaya stands up behind the 108 chortens. Snow falls on the high passes and occasionally closes one for a day, but in the western valleys it rarely lies long. Punakha stays mild, which is why the central monk body moves down to the dzong there for the winter.

Winter is the season of the black-necked cranes. They arrive in the Phobjikha valley from late October and leave in February, and the Royal Society for Protection of Nature counts roughly 300 each year, making it the largest wintering ground in the country. The Black-necked Crane Festival is held at Gangtey Goenpa on 11 November every year, with dances by monks and by children from the valley schools. Trongsa Tshechu falls in December or January, from 17 to 21 December in 2026, and the Punakha festivals come in late February.
Hotels are quieter, and the light is clear for photography. Pack for real cold in Bumthang and Phobjikha, where hotel rooms rely on heaters and nights fall well below freezing.

For high treks there are two windows. Spring, from April to May, brings flowers but less reliable views and the chance of late snow on the passes. Autumn, from late September to November, is drier and clearer and is the season most trekkers choose. Summer treks are wet and muddy, and in winter the highest passes can close. That is why we walk the Jomolhari route in autumn only.

items: A mindfulness journey through the sacred valleys: spring and autumn, when the long walks and the drives over the passes are at their best.
Meditation and Buddhist practice: year round, since the practice does not depend on the view.
Sacred rhythms, a festival and meditation journey: timed to a tshechu, so the dates follow the lunar calendar.
Paro Tshechu, a cultural and nature journey: built around the Paro festival each spring.
The Jomolhari trek: autumn only.

title: Planning a first journey to Bhutan
standfirst: How travel to Bhutan works as of 2026: licensed guides, the online visa, the US$ 100 Sustainable Development Fee, flights into Paro, and what to arrange when.

body.body: Bhutan does not work like most places you fly to on holiday. Nobody arrives on spec with a rucksack and a guidebook. The visa, the guide, the vehicle, the hotels and the permits for each valley are arranged before you land, and none of it is difficult once you know the order it happens in.

This guide sets out that order as it stands in 2026. Fees and rules here are set by government and do change, so everything below is checked each season, and the figures that apply to your journey are confirmed in the notes we send when it is booked.

Every international visitor travels with a licensed Bhutanese guide. The Department of Tourism is direct about it: a guide must accompany you at all times, and that includes travellers who drive their own car in over a land border. Guides, tour operators and hotels are certified by the Department and listed on its public services portal, so you can check that the people you are dealing with hold a licence.

Since the tourism reforms of 2022 you may in principle arrange a guide, hotels and transport yourself rather than through an operator. Most travellers still book with a licensed operator, who puts the pieces together, applies for the visa and carries responsibility for all of it on the ground. On our journeys the guide is Bhutanese and licensed, and travels with you from the airport on the first day to the airport on the last.

The guide matters more than any hotel. He or she is the person who explains the mural you are standing in front of, knows when a dzong closes to visitors for the afternoon, and arranges the time with a Lam. It is worth asking an operator who your guide will be and what they know well.

Visitors from every country except India, Bangladesh and the Maldives, which have their own arrangements, apply for a visa online before they travel. Your operator or hotel can lodge the application on your behalf, or you can do it yourself through the Department of Immigration's system. You need a digital copy of your passport, a recent digital passport photograph and your dates of arrival and departure.

The visa fee is paid at the same time as the Sustainable Development Fee for your nights in the country, and the Department of Tourism says a correctly completed application takes up to five working days. The approval comes back as a document you carry with you and show when you check in for the flight to Paro and again at immigration. A passport valid for at least six months beyond your journey is the usual expectation, so check yours before anything else.

body.title: The visa, as of 2026
rows: Your operator or hotel, or you, online
Passport copy, recent photo, travel dates
The SDF for every night you stay

body.body: The Sustainable Development Fee, the SDF, is a daily levy paid by every visitor for each night spent in Bhutan. As of 2026 it is US$ 100 per adult per night. In 2023 the government halved it from US$ 200 and said the reduced rate would hold for four years, so the current figure is set to run into 2027. Travellers from India pay a separate rate in ngultrum.

Children pay less. Those aged six and not yet twelve pay US$ 50 a night, and children under six pay nothing. The fee is paid in advance with the visa, which is why an operator will ask for final dates before it applies.

The Department of Tourism describes the SDF as funding free healthcare and education, training for people who work in tourism, infrastructure and the protection of the environment. It is the practical side of the country's long-standing preference for fewer visitors who each contribute more, and it is one reason the valleys you travel through are not crowded.

body.title: SDF, as of 2026
rows: In advance, with the visa application

body.body: Paro has the country's only international airport, and two Bhutanese airlines fly into it: Drukair, the national carrier, and the privately owned Bhutan Airlines. As of 2026 Drukair flies from Bangkok, Kolkata and Kathmandu most days, with fewer weekly flights from Delhi, Singapore, Dhaka, Guwahati and Dubai, and seasonal services from Gaya and Bagdogra. Bhutan Airlines flies from Bangkok, Kolkata, Kathmandu and Delhi. Schedules change by season, and neither airline flies every route every day.

Seats are limited, so the flight into Paro is usually booked before anything else is fixed. It is almost always a separate ticket from your long-haul flight, which means a missed connection is your problem rather than the airline's. We suggest a night in the hub city on the way in. The landing itself comes down between forested ridges onto the valley floor, and the airlines keep it to daylight hours with pilots trained for the approach.

Inside the country, Drukair also flies short domestic hops from Paro, including to Bumthang in the centre, which takes about 35 minutes and saves a long day on the road. Our sacred valleys journey flies out to Bumthang early on and drives back west through the valleys.

It is also possible to enter by road from India. Phuentsholing is the main crossing, with Gelephu and Samdrup Jongkhar further east. The same guide rule applies from the moment you travel beyond the border town, and the drive up to Thimphu from Phuentsholing takes most of a day.
Prices in Bhutan are quoted in different ways, and it is worth knowing exactly what a figure covers before you compare two of them. On our journeys the price includes:
