Every meal, with tea or coffee
Accommodation in family-run hotels
Your guide, and the guide's transport, food, lodging and insurance
A down jacket, all-season sleeping bag and duffel bag, on loan
All permits and paperwork within Bhutan
On the Jomolhari trek, all camping equipment, the crew, cook, ponies and pony handlers

body.body: It does not include international flights, visa charges, travel and medical insurance, personal spending, or emergency costs such as a chartered helicopter. Our prices include the SDF. Some operators quote it separately, so make sure any two figures you compare treat it the same way. Since 1 January 2026 a 5% goods and services tax applies to most services in Bhutan, and the journey notes show how it is handled in your price.

Bhutan withdrew its requirement for compulsory travel insurance on 23 April 2024, and the Department of Tourism still strongly recommends it. We go further and ask every traveller to take cover before they come. The Royal Insurance Corporation of Bhutan runs a plan for visitors, or you can use your own insurer at home.

Whichever you choose, read the policy for two things. It should cover emergency evacuation, including by helicopter, since that is the cost that can run into thousands. If you are walking the Jomolhari trek, it should cover trekking to 4,930 m, because many standard policies stop well below that.

items: Nine to twelve months ahead: choose the journey and the season. Festival journeys follow the lunar calendar, so ask for the coming dates before you settle on a month.
Six to nine months ahead: book the flight into Paro and out again, then the long-haul flights around it, with a night's buffer in the hub.
At the same time: check your passport's expiry date and the name on it matches your tickets exactly.

Two to three months ahead: see your doctor or a travel clinic. Tetanus, typhoid and hepatitis A are the usual recommendations, and it is the moment to talk about altitude if you have any medical condition.
Six to eight weeks ahead: arrange insurance, and send us your passport copy and photo so the visa can be lodged with the SDF.
The last fortnight: print the visa approval, read the journey notes, and pack for a thousand metres of difference between one valley and the next.

body.body: None of this needs to be done alone. Once a journey is booked we handle the visa, the SDF and the permits, and the notes we send confirm every fee and date as it stands for your departure.

title: Eleven days in the sacred valleys
standfirst: How our sacred valleys journey is put together: a flight east to Bumthang on the second morning, then ten days working slowly back west by road to Paro and the walk to Taktsang.

body.body: Many journeys in Bhutan begin in Paro, push east by road and then drive back the way they came. This one turns that around. It spends a single night in Paro, flies to Bumthang in the centre of the country, and then drives west, valley by valley, until it is back where it started. No road is driven twice, and every day brings you a little closer to the airport you leave from.

That shape decides almost everything else about the journey: how long the drives are, where the rest day falls, and why the hardest walk of the eleven days is kept until the tenth. The days below are the journey as it runs on a typical departure.

body.title: At a glance
rows: 5 h, Punakha to Paro via Thimphu

body.body: The journey starts at 2,200 m on the floor of the Paro valley. There is no climbing on the first day, only two temples. Dungtse Lhakhang was built by the iron-bridge builder Thangtong Gyalpo in the fifteenth century in the form of a chorten, which is rare in Bhutan, and it holds fine murals. Kyichu Lhakhang is older still: tradition places its founding in the seventh century, under the Tibetan king Songtsen Gampo.

After that the afternoon is left open. The arrival flight is early, the air is thinner than most travellers are used to, and a first day that asks very little of you is the best preparation for the ten that follow.

On the second morning a short domestic flight carries the group east to Bumthang, at about 2,600 m. It takes a little over half an hour; the same distance by road is a full day's drive or more. Flying out at the start is the reason the rest of the journey can be driven in comfortable stages rather than in one long push.

Domestic flights in the mountains depend on the weather, and a cloudy morning can mean waiting. Your guide will explain the alternatives on the day if the valley is closed in. Once you land, Jakar Dzong, the Castle of the White Bird, is on its ridge above the valley, and it is the first visit.

Bumthang is where Buddhism in Bhutan has its oldest roots, and the journey gives it three nights. The first full day is a round of its sacred sites. Mebar Tsho, the burning lake, is a pool in a gorge of the Tang Chhu where, tradition holds, the treasure revealer Pema Lingpa dived with a lamp in his hand and surfaced with the lamp still alight. Kurjey Lhakhang is built around the rock where Guru Rinpoche meditated. Tamshing, across the river, was founded by Pema Lingpa himself, and Jambay Lhakhang is counted among the oldest temples in the country.

The day ends at Kharchu Monastery, a Nyingma monastery above Jakar founded in the late twentieth century by Namkhai Nyingpo Rinpoche. The young monks gather in the evening for prayers, and visitors sit at the back of the hall and listen.

The next day is quieter. A slow drive climbs to Tharpaling, at 3,600 m in the Chhume valley, a monastery associated with the fourteenth-century teacher Longchenpa. There are prayer halls and murals, and monks going about the ordinary rituals of the day. The itinerary gives this visit one instruction: time to sit. Resident Lams lead the sitting in the monasteries along the way; your guide handles everything else.

body.text: The road west: Trongsa and Phobjikha

body.body: On day five the driving begins. Bumthang to Trongsa is about four hours through rolling hills and small villages, and it ends at Trongsa Dzong, the long fortress on its ridge above the Mangde Chhu that for centuries stood over the only road between east and west. There is time for the courtyards, the temples and the woodwork.

Day six is another four hours, over the passes and down into Phobjikha, a broad glacial valley at about 2,900 m. The afternoon takes in Gangtey Goenpa above the village and the smaller Drechakling, and then a first walk on the valley floor. This is the winter ground of the black-necked cranes, which arrive in late October; a late autumn departure may find the first of them already there.

Day seven is the rest day, and it is written in on purpose. There are trails across the meadows, through pine forest and past farmhouses, and nobody is keeping time. You can walk all of it or none of it. It is the one day of the eleven with nothing in it at all.

body.text: Punakha, and the long drive home

body.body: From Phobjikha it is three hours down to Punakha, which sits much lower and warmer than anywhere else on the route. Punakha Dzong stands where the Pho Chhu and the Mo Chhu meet, reached by a roofed cantilever bridge. In the afternoon there is Chimi Lhakhang, the temple associated with Drukpa Kunley, and at dusk a walk along the river.

Day nine is the longest drive, about five hours. The road climbs back over Dochula and drops into Thimphu, where the journey stops for Tashichho Dzong and for Buddha Dordenma on the ridge above the capital, before going on to Paro for a calm evening.

The walk to Taktsang is the one day on this journey that asks something of your legs. It climbs through pine forest and past small waterfalls to 3,120 m, and the round trip takes about five hours, returning by the same path. Placing it on day ten means you arrive at the foot of the cliff with nine days at altitude behind you, including three nights in Bumthang and a visit to 3,600 m at Tharpaling. By then the climb is steady rather than hard.

There is also a simpler reason. Taktsang is the most revered site in the Paro valley, and after ten days of monasteries, prayer halls and sitting, it reads differently than it would on the second morning. Day eleven is a slow breakfast and the short transfer to the airport.

The drives are never longer than five hours, and they are not treated as dead time. Mindfulness of feeling and sensation is practised on every drive: noticing the body in the seat, the turns of the road, the change in the air as the valleys drop and rise. It is taught plainly and it is always optional.

items: Mornings start without hurry, and no day has both a long drive and a long walk.
Sitting practice is woven into the monastery visits rather than scheduled as a separate class.
Accommodation is in family-run hotels, and every meal is included.
The journey supports Osel Ling Perila Goenpa, a monastery in the hills above Paro, with thirty per cent of what you pay.

body.body: Dress for the temples each day: long sleeves and long trousers or a skirt, hats off inside, and shoes off at the door of a temple room. Photography is not allowed inside most lhakhangs and your guide will say where it is.

Departures are in spring and autumn. Spring brings rhododendron on the passes and the jacaranda in Punakha; autumn brings clear air, harvested fields and, late in the season, the first cranes in Phobjikha. The Sustainable Development Fee, set by the government, is US$ 100 per person per night as of 2026. Fees, flight schedules and entry rules are checked each season and confirmed in the journey notes we send when a departure is booked.
